claims.text: Premelting and melting in high-entropy-alloy nanoparticles are primarily governed by local compositional heterogeneity.
Local compositional heterogeneity induces lattice strain at nanoparticle surfaces.
Surface lattice strain lowers the local energy barrier for atomic mobility.
Lower barriers for surface atomic mobility reduce the effective melting temperature.
High chemical complexity creates localized regions with less-uniform atomic packing and enhanced lattice strain.
Strained regions are particularly prevalent at the nanoparticle surface.
Strained surface regions permit premelting below the bulk melting point.
Premelted or mobile surface regions expand as temperature increases.
Expansion of the strained or premelted regions lowers the overall nanoparticle melting temperature.
Nanoparticles engineered with greater near-surface compositional heterogeneity and associated strain will have a lower premelting-onset temperature than a chemically homogeneous baseline.
Nanoparticles engineered with greater near-surface compositional heterogeneity and associated strain will have a lower overall melting temperature than a chemically homogeneous baseline.
The predicted thermal changes will appear as shifted DSC endotherms.
The predicted premelting change will appear as earlier surface disordering in in situ TEM images.
The proposed relationship is expected to hold for nanoparticles between 2 and 30 nm containing at least five principal elements in near-equal molar ratios.
Outside the stated size or compositional-complexity range, extreme size effects or phase separation may dominate premelting and melting behavior.
Particle size and surface-energy variations may interact with the relationship between compositional heterogeneity and melting-temperature reduction.

Failure of the heterogeneous series to show statistically significant reductions in both premelting onset and overall melting temperature relative to the homogeneous control would falsify the hypothesis.

contradictions.description: The intervention treats intentional ordering as an example of increased compositional heterogeneity, although ordering can instead reduce local chemical disorder. The direction of the mediator change is therefore not consistently specified.
